# V100-106 — Linters as an acceptance gate: how much generated code passes first time

_Measured on a Tesla V100-SXM2 16 GB (sm_70) inside a virtual machine: 24 vCPU, 94 GiB RAM, driver 580.178.04._

**Question.** Code from these cards goes to a client, not into a drawer, so the acceptance gate matters more than the model's taste. Can static checks be that gate? The card criterion: at least 70% of generated files pass the linter with no edits, otherwise every order carries manual clean-up hours that must be priced in.

**Environment.**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| GPU | Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB, compute capability 7.0, 16384 MiB |
| Driver | 580.178.04 |
| Engine | llama.cpp 1.0.0-dev, build 12359, commit b1b770d90 (`/home/hermes/llama-new/build129/bin/llama-server`) |
| Model | Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct-Q8_0 (8.1 GB) |
| Host | Ubuntu 24.04, 24 vCPU, 94 GiB RAM |
| Linters | ruff 0.17.6 (`check --select E,F`), mypy 2.4.1 (`--ignore-missing-imports`) in `/root/venvs/lint` |
| Tasks | MBPP, 40 tasks, each run against its own `test_list` with a 20 s timeout |

**Commands.** Driver script under the runner, then one server per run and three checks per task:

```
/root/bin/v100-run.sh V100-106 -- python3 /root/lint106.py

/home/hermes/llama-new/build129/bin/llama-server -m /srv/media/ai-cache/downloads/qwen7b-quants/qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q8_0.gguf \
  --port 18360 -ngl 99 -c 4096 --jinja --no-webui -t 8

ruff check --select E,F --output-format json /root/runs/V100-106/src/task_NNN.py
mypy --ignore-missing-imports --no-error-summary /root/runs/V100-106/src/task_NNN.py
python -c "<generated code>\n\n<task test_list>"      # 20 s timeout, rc=0 means the tests pass
```

Requests go to `/v1/chat/completions` with `max_tokens` 512 and `temperature` 0; the code is cut out of the first fenced block and lines starting with `>>>`, `Input:` or `Output:` are dropped before linting.

**Results.**

| Metric | Value | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Tasks generated | 40 | - |
| Tests pass | 24 | 0.60 |
| ruff clean (`E,F`) | 39 | 0.975 |
| mypy clean (`--ignore-missing-imports`) | 40 | 1.00 |
| Clean under both linters | 39 | 0.975 |
| Clean under both linters and tests pass | 24 | 0.60 |
| ruff findings in the whole sample | 1 | - |
| mypy errors in the whole sample | 0 | - |

**Result.** The criterion is met with room to spare: 39 of 40 files are lint-clean and the only ruff finding in the sample is a single issue, against a threshold of 70%. The acceptance gap sits elsewhere, in behaviour: the same files pass their tests only 24 times out of 40. mypy's 40 of 40 is not a quality signal at all here, because the generated code carries no type annotations, so there is almost nothing for the checker to verify. The honest reading is that syntax-level cleanliness is free, and a gate built only on linters would pass 39 files that behave correctly in 24 cases.

**Verdict.** Static checks are not the bottleneck: lint cleanliness is nearly free for this model (39/40), while the behaviour of the same code passes tests only 24/40, so tests must be the acceptance gate and linters only a hygiene filter.

**Result type.** Mixed.

**Does not show.** Only Python was measured: eslint/tsc for TypeScript, `go vet`/staticcheck for Go and phpstan for PHP are untouched, so the "lint is free" conclusion does not transfer to those languages. mypy ran without annotations and without `--strict`, so type-level quality is unmeasured; a task statement that demands annotations and `--strict` would be a different experiment. MBPP prompts are function-sized, not project-sized, and the number of manual edits per file (as opposed to pass/fail) was not counted, so the clean-up hours behind the 70% criterion are still an estimate.

**Follow-up.** The `mypy --strict` arm with annotations required in the prompt is the missing half of this card and is not queued yet; when it lands, the lint column here gets rewritten with the strict numbers.
